extracted.intended_audience: law students, judges, and patent practitioners studying novelty and utility doctrines
extracted.subtask_description: Foundational criteria and tests for whether an alleged invention satisfies the statutory requirements of novelty and utility (and the sufficiency of invention) for patentability, illustrated with case law. Focuses on what counts as a 'new' and 'useful' invention, claim scope, prior use, combinations, and evidence burdens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility requirement ('useful')
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject of a patent must be 'useful' — capable of use and not mischievous, frivolous, or injurious to the well-being, good policy or sound morals of society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Utility means capability of use for some beneficial purpose; the degree (large or small) of utility is not decisive for sufficiency of invention. An invention that is merely deceptive, or only improves the art of selling (e.g., packaging/labeling that does not alter the article), is not a valid 'useful' invention. Courts examine circumstances of each case to determine whether the subject-matter is capable of use to the public's advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty requirement ('new')
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject of a patent must be 'new' — a new art, machine, manufacture, composition of matter, or a 'new improvement' upon one of these 'not known or used by others' before.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty requires the claimed subject-matter be substantially different from anything known or used before. When analogous or similar things existed, the 'substantial difference' is the measure of sufficiency. Courts focus on the character of the result produced rather than the apparent amount of skill or ingenuity exercised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of invention measured by result (not amount of skill)
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining sufficiency of invention, courts examine the character of the result, and not the apparent amount of skill, ingenuity or thought exercised; a substantially different result from what existed before supports patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even simple inventions can be of the highest value; the simplicity or ease of accomplishing it is not an obstacle if the result is new and substantial. Evidence that a defendant's invention is 'better' is only relevant to show substantive difference between inventions, not as a general endorsement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change of form/proportion doctrine (must produce new effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: A mere change of form or proportions of a known machine or composition is not a 'discovery' unless the change produces a different effect or principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The word 'simply' (in 'simply changing the form or the proportions') is important: only changes that do more than alter form/proportion — i.e., produce a new effect or principle — can constitute patentable invention. Courts ask whether the change has produced a different effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentable subject is the mode/manner of producing an effect, not the effect alone
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent cannot be for an effect only (e.g., the admeasurement of time or expansive operations of steam) but only for a new mode or new application of machinery to produce these effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents cover a particular manner, device, or modus operandi producing an effect. If the same effects are produced by unaltered old machinery, there is no invention; but if the principles/mode of operation are new, the whole machine may be patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims limited to the actual invention — whole machine vs improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: If a specific machine already exists producing certain effects, merely adding an improvement does not entitle the patentee to a patent for the whole machine — only for the actual improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patent cannot be broader than the inventor's contribution. Combining previously separate operations into one machine does not make the whole machine new unless the principles of operation themselves are new. Examples: lever in a watch or Watt's improvements do not permit patents covering the whole machine beyond the actual improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination inventions: new combination may be patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: A combination of materials or known elements can be patentable if the combination as arranged is new and produces a new result; ingredients need not individually be novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The test is whether the materials have been used in the same combination before. If the result produced by the particular combination is new, that suffices for sufficiency of invention even if the combination appears simple. Jury fact-finding will often determine whether such a combination was known or used before.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of old contrivance to new purpose is not invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying an old apparatus or machinery to a new purpose, without any new means or adaptation, does not constitute a patentable invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The end or purpose itself is not patentable; what is patentable is the adaptation of materials or new apparatus by which the purpose is accomplished. Examples: using existing coffee-mill to grind different grain, or applying an unaltered loom to a different yarn, is not patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior public knowledge or use by others defeats novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject-matter must not have been 'known or used by others' before the discovery or invention by the patentee; prior use by even one other person is sufficient to show the patentee was not the first inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: U.S. construction focuses on prior knowledge/use by others (not the inventor). The timing and character of such knowledge or use is crucial — public disclosure or use before the patentee's discovery can invalidate the patent. Distinction with English law: in England any prior knowledge at any time can invalidate; U.S. interpretation is shaped by the policy to give public rights as early as possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of prior use or knowledge matters
rubrics_metrics.description: The time at which knowledge or use by others occurred that will vitiate a patent is an important point and affects validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under U.S. law (as interpreted in the text), the relevant prior knowledge/use is that which existed before the discovery by the patentee. Courts examine whether the prior use was public and whether it predates the inventor's discovery/application in a manner that defeats novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent is prima facie evidence of novelty (patentee's oath)
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent and the statutory oath by the applicant that he 'verily believes himself to be the original and first inventor or discoverer' is prima facie evidence of novelty, placing the onus on the party challenging novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slight evidence from the patentee of what his invention consists of is sufficient initially; once offered, the burden (onus probandi) shifts to the defendant to prove want of novelty. The patent's recitation of the oath is evidence of the inventor's claim to originality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court's fact-based inquiry into whether effects were produced before
rubrics_metrics.description: When a patent claims multiple stages or combined effects, the question is whether any of those effects were produced in earlier machines by combinations or modes of operation substantially the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If earlier machinery produced any of the distinct effects by substantially the same means, the claim for the whole machine may be invalid and at most cover the improvement only. Juries often decide whether principles or modes of operation are 'altogether new' or merely improvements on prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public policy balancing: encourage prompt disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislative and judicial construction of prior-use and novelty rules reflect a policy that rewards prompt disclosure to the public and avoids allowing inventors to indefinitely delay public knowledge while exploiting an invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The law disfavors permitting an inventor to commercially exploit an invention for years and then secure a patent to exclude the public; this rationale informs limits on what prior use/knowledge will defeat a later patent and why 'not known or used by others before' is interpreted strictly.
